**7B.5 Research Note: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2024**

Best-supported reading: mixed, but tilted negative. Sisi did make a visible technocratic cabinet reshuffle and issued some pro-institution language, yet the year also shows heavy reliance on trusted security insiders, weak independent oversight, and continued politicization of state institutions. I did not find reliable 2024 evidence that he was filling government with family members or donor-clients specifically; the stronger evidence is for loyalists and embedded security elites, not a clean family-crony patronage trail.

### Accepted claims

| Title | Publisher | Date | URL | Claim-level summary | QIDs |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| President Sisi swears in new government ministers | State Information Service | Jul. 3, 2024 | https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/president-sisi-swears-in-new-government-ministers/ | The reshuffle installed a broad cabinet with technocratic portfolios tied to economic management, energy, science, and foreign affairs. This is the strongest pro-competence evidence I found for 2024 appointments. | 7B.5 |
| President El-Sisi meets prime minister and members of the new government | State Information Service | Jul. 3, 2024 | https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/president-el-sisi-meets-prime-minister-and-members-of-the-new-government/ | Sisi told the new government to strengthen institutional frameworks, improve inter-agency coordination, and emphasize integrity and transparency. That is direct pro-professionalization language, though it is official self-reporting. | 7B.5, 7B.2 |
| Egypt - United States Department of State | U.S. Department of State | 2024 | https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/2024-investment-climate-statements/egypt/ | The report says SOEs and military-owned companies still enjoy significant advantages and that private firms complain about inconsistent enforcement. This supports the view that appointments and institutions still protected regime-connected interests rather than neutral administration. | 7B.5, 7B.4 |
| OECD Economic Surveys: Egypt 2024 | OECD | 2024 | https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-egypt-2024_af900de2-en/full-report/component-8.html | OECD says military-owned firms benefit from tax and land/resource advantages, ownership and management selection is opaque, and public ownership structures are not transparent. This is strong evidence against a clean meritocratic governing style. | 7B.5, 7B.4 |
| Egypt’s new cabinet members sworn in after major reshuffle | The National | Jul. 3, 2024 | https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2024/07/03/egypts-new-cabinet-members-sworn-in-after-major-reshuffle/ | Coverage described the new cabinet as focused on economic reform and national security challenges. This is weaker than the official Egyptian statement, but still consistent with a more technocratic framing than pure cronyism. | 7B.5 |
| Egypt’s Sisi names ex-defence minister and chief of staff as advisers after reshuffle | Reuters via Yahoo | Jul. 3, 2024 | https://www.yahoo.com/news/egypts-sisi-names-ex-defence-140545714.html | Reuters reported that Sisi replaced the defense minister and chief of staff, then moved both outgoing officials into presidential adviser roles. That looks like managed insider recycling, not a decisive break toward independent professional staffing. | 7B.5 |
| Egypt’s Sisi replaces head of powerful general intelligence agency | Reuters via The National | Oct. 16, 2024 | https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2024/10/16/el-sisi-names-new-chief-of-intelligence-agency-replacing-long-time-close-aide-and-confidant/ | Sisi replaced the intelligence chief with his deputy and kept the outgoing chief close as an adviser. The continuation of a tightly embedded security network cuts against a clean technocratic interpretation. | 7B.5 |
| Egypt’s Al-Sisi has caged himself | Human Rights Watch | Feb. 26, 2024 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/02/26/egypts-al-sisi-has-caged-himself | HRW argues Sisi relies on coercion and the military/security services rather than a normal party structure, and that independent institutions have been hollowed out. This is strong negative evidence on appointing autonomous professionals. | 7B.5, 7B.3 |
| Egypt: Civic space under siege | Human Rights Watch | Jan. 11, 2024 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/egypt-civic-space-under-siege | HRW says authorities curtailed free expression and peaceful assembly ahead of the presidential vote to stymie competition. That suggests institutions were still being used to protect incumbency, not to empower neutral professionals. | 7B.5, 7B.2 |
| Freedom in the World 2024: Egypt | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/egypt/freedom-world/2024 | Freedom House says Sisi and the security apparatus dominate policymaking, parliament lacks a meaningful check, and the corruption watchdog is controlled by Sisi. This points to personal control over institutions rather than professional independence. | 7B.5, 7B.4 |

### Search gap

- I did not find reliable 2024 evidence that Sisi appointed close family members to cabinet or major state posts.
- I also did not find a clean 2024 paper trail of donor appointments or business-associate patronage at the level of named officeholders.
- The evidence is therefore mostly structural: competent technocrats in some civilian portfolios, but loyalty-heavy rotation and security-state continuity at the top.

### Bottom line

- **Pro-competence evidence exists**: the July 2024 cabinet reshuffle, technocratic portfolio assignments, and official rhetoric about coordination and transparency.
- **Stronger contrary evidence exists**: trusted insiders were recycled into advisory posts, the intelligence/security apparatus stayed politically embedded, and independent oversight remained weak.
- For 7B.5, I would treat 2024 as **mixed but leaning negative**: some technocratic staffing, but not enough to show Sisi had genuinely shifted away from loyalist, personalist control.
